title: CAP & PACELC
subtitle: Cut the link between two replicas and watch the system be forced to choose between answering and being right.
learn: What CAP really says: during a network partition you give up consistency or availability
Why partitions are a fact of life, not an option you can decline
How PACELC adds the everyday trade-off: latency versus consistency when nothing is broken
The difference between strong, causal, and eventual consistency, with examples
How to pick a model per feature instead of per whole system

steps.title: Two copies of one value
steps.body: A profile setting x is stored on two replicas: A in the US and B in Europe, so each user reads from a nearby copy. Both hold x = 4. Alice sets x = 5 on A. Bob, in Europe, reads x from B a moment later. What should Bob see, and what if the link between A and B is cut right now?
steps.idea: Copying data to two places creates a question: which copy is allowed to be behind?
steps.caption: Alice writes x = 5 to A; B still holds x = 4.

steps.title: Healthy network: easy
steps.body: With the link up, A forwards x = 5 to B and waits for B's acknowledgement before telling Alice it worked. Now any read from either replica returns 5. This is strong consistency: the system behaves as if there were one copy. The price is that Alice waits for a transatlantic round trip, roughly 80 ms, on top of the local write.
steps.idea: When nothing is broken you can have both consistency and availability; you just pay latency for it.
steps.caption: A copies to B and waits for the ack before replying.

steps.title: The link breaks
steps.body: Now a fibre cut or a bad router config severs the path between the regions. Both replicas are healthy and both users can still reach their nearest copy, but A and B cannot talk. This is a network partition. Neither side can tell whether the other is dead or just unreachable. You cannot design partitions away: any system spread over a network will eventually see one.
steps.idea: Partitions are not a choice. CAP is about what you do once one happens.
steps.caption: A and B are both up but cannot reach each other.

steps.title: Option 1: stay correct, refuse
steps.body: A consistency-first (CP) system protects the single-copy illusion. A cannot confirm that B will see the write, so it rejects Alice's request with an error. B likewise refuses reads it cannot prove are current. Nobody ever sees stale or conflicting data, but during the partition users get errors. Real CP systems with three or more replicas keep serving on the side that still has a majority; the minority side stops.
steps.idea: Choosing consistency means some requests fail while the partition lasts.
steps.caption: A returns an error rather than accept a write B cannot see.

steps.title: Option 2: stay up, diverge
steps.body: An availability-first (AP) system keeps answering. A accepts x = 5 and replies instantly, since it does not wait for B. But Bob's read from B returns the old value 4: stale, and still a valid answer because B is up. If Bob had also written x on B, the two copies would now hold different values that must be reconciled later.
steps.idea: Choosing availability means replicas can disagree while the partition lasts.
steps.caption: A accepts the write; B serves the old value x = 4.

steps.title: The link comes back
steps.body: When the partition heals, an AP system must converge. A sends the missed update to B, and B applies it, so both hold 5 again. This is eventual consistency: if writes stop, all replicas end up equal. The hard case is two conflicting writes made on both sides. Deciding which wins, or merging them, is covered in the clocks and CRDT lessons.
steps.idea: Eventual consistency promises convergence, not when, and not which concurrent write survives.
steps.caption: A pushes the missed write to B; copies converge.

steps.title: Even with no partition
steps.body: CAP only talks about failures, but partitions are rare and the trade-off is constant. PACELC extends it: if Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. In the healthy case, a strongly consistent write waits for the far replica. With about 80 ms between regions, every write pays about 80 ms extra, on every request, not only during outages.
steps.idea: PACELC: the everyday cost of consistency is latency, paid even when everything works.
steps.caption: Synchronous replication: Alice waits for B's ack.

steps.title: Else: pick latency
steps.body: The alternative is asynchronous replication. A confirms to Alice after its own write, taking about 5 ms, then ships x = 5 to B in the background. Writes are 17 times faster, but for the next 80 ms or more Bob can still read 4. Databases in the Dynamo style are typically PA/EL (availability, then latency); Google Spanner is PC/EC (consistency both times).
steps.idea: Async replication buys speed by letting replicas briefly lag. Sync replication buys correctness with delay.
steps.caption: A replies at once and replicates in the background.

steps.title: A ladder of consistency
steps.body: Consistency is a spectrum. Strong (linearizable): every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were one copy. Causal: if one event could have influenced another, everyone sees them in that order. Alice posts a question and Bob replies; nobody may see the reply before the question. Eventual: replicas only converge over time, with no ordering promise. Weaker models are cheaper and faster.
steps.idea: Pick the weakest model your feature can tolerate; each step up costs latency or availability.
steps.caption: Post then reply must appear in order under causal consistency.

steps.title: How to think about it
steps.body: CAP: when a partition splits the replicas, choose consistency (reject some requests) or availability (accept and diverge). It is not pick-two-of-three, because partitions will happen. PACELC: even without one, choose latency or consistency. Decide per feature: a bank balance and a unique username need strong consistency; a like counter or a feed can be eventual.
steps.idea: Ask two questions: what happens during a partition, and what latency am I paying when it is healthy?
steps.caption: All four parts: clients, two replicas, and the link between.

quiz.q: A three-replica database splits into a group of 2 and a lone replica. The lone replica rejects all writes. In CAP terms, what did the system choose?
options: Availability on every node
Consistency, giving up availability on the minority side
It gave up partition tolerance
Neither; this is not a CAP situation
quiz.why: Refusing writes that cannot be safely replicated preserves a single history (consistency) at the cost of the isolated node being unavailable. This is the CP choice.

quiz.q: A teammate says: 'We chose CA, so we never have to worry about partitions.' What is the flaw?
options: CA systems cannot have more than one replica
Network partitions happen regardless; you only decide how the system behaves when one occurs
Availability is impossible without partition tolerance
CAP only applies to NoSQL databases
quiz.why: On any real network, partitions happen whether you plan for them or not. A 'CA' design just has undefined or accidental behavior when one occurs.

quiz.q: Cross-region round trip is 80 ms. A service with no failures at all still sees 80 ms added to every write. Which idea explains this?
options: The C in CAP, applied during partitions
PACELC's 'else' branch: consistency costs latency even when healthy
Eventual consistency
Causal ordering
quiz.why: Waiting for a distant replica to acknowledge is the latency price of strong consistency, paid on every write even without a partition.

quiz.q: In a social app, Bob sees a reply to Alice's comment but not the comment itself. Which guarantee would prevent this?
options: Eventual consistency
Causal consistency
Higher availability
Faster replication hardware
quiz.why: Causal consistency ensures that if one event could have caused another, every reader sees them in that order. Plain eventual consistency allows the reply to arrive first.

quiz.q: Which feature most clearly needs strong consistency rather than eventual?
options: View count on a video
Claiming a unique username at signup
Number of followers shown on a profile
Recently viewed items list
quiz.why: Two replicas accepting the same username concurrently would break uniqueness. Counters and recency lists tolerate being briefly stale.

cheatsheet.def: During a network partition, a replicated system can keep consistency or availability, not both. Partitions are not optional.
Linearizability: every read returns the latest completed write, as if there were a single copy. Not the same as ACID consistency.
Every non-failing node answers every request with a non-error response, even if the data is stale.
If Partition: Availability or Consistency; Else: Latency or Consistency. Captures the everyday cost of strong guarantees.
Reads see the latest write. Needs coordination between replicas, so it costs round trips and can reject requests in a partition.
Related events (a question and its reply) are seen in order by everyone; unrelated events may appear in any order.
If writes stop, replicas converge. No promise about when, or about reads in the meantime. Fast and highly available.
Choose consistency per feature: money, uniqueness, and inventory lean strong; counters, feeds, and caches lean eventual.
